title: cheniere energy report rise second quarter profit 2026 08 06
text:
Aug 6 (Reuters) - Cheniere Energy (LNG.N)
, opens new tab
 raised its forecast for annual ‌core profit on Thursday after beating quarterly expectations on robust LNG demand and high output, sending its shares up 3.5% in early afternoon trading.
The largest U.S. LNG exporter expects adjusted core profit to range from $7.9 billion to $8.4 billion in 2026, compared with its prior ​projection of $7.25 billion to $7.75 billion.
The Houston, Texas-based company's adjusted core profit for the second quarter was $1.8 billion, ​beating analyst expectations of $1.72 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.
"We don't see these ⁠financial results as one-off going forward once LNG prices stabilize," the company's chief financial officer, Zach Davis, said ​during an earnings call.
He said increased output would offset any declines in margins that have been elevated by ongoing disruptions ​in the Middle East.
Cheniere said it exported 184 cargoes of LNG in the three months ended June 30, up 19.4% from a year earlier. The company expects increased exports next year as it will have a full year of production from its expansion ​projects, Davis said.
Cheniere received authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in June to increase LNG production capacity ​at its Corpus Christi Stage 3 and CCL Midscale Trains 8 and 9 projects in Texas by around 5 million tonnes ‌per ⁠annum combined.
Cheniere raised the bottom of its full-year production forecast to 53 million tonnes from 52 million, keeping the top of the range at 54 million.
Cheniere chief commercial officer Anatol Feygin said Europe is in a very difficult position going into winter as its natural gas storage levels remain low. Each additional month ​of constrained flows through the ​Strait of Hormuz — a result ⁠of the U.S.-Iran war — could reduce the region's storage position by approximately five percentage points, he added.
Disruptions in the Middle East are still affecting output, but Feygin said ​there had not been widespread demand destruction for LNG because China's flexibility mitigated much of the ​supply shock, adding ⁠he did not expect China to allow its natural gas storage levels to fall to the same extent as Europe.
U.S. LNG deliveries to Asia hit a quarterly record of 11 million metric tons in the second quarter, as exporters ⁠chased ​prices that were running above Europe's, Feygin said.
Cheniere is in talks ​with prospective buyers and believes it can still command between $2.50 and $3 per mmBtu for liquefaction fees on new contracts, Feygin said, despite heavy ​competition from other U.S. LNG developers.
